newsitem.title: USA: Stadium bonds bill not high priority now - D'Amato.
newsitem.headline: Stadium bonds bill not high priority now - D'Amato.

text.p: U.S. Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, said on Wednesday he has not formed an opinion yet on controversial legislation to bar tax-exempt financing for professional sports stadiums and that the measure is not currently a "high priority" in the Senate.
"I have not formed an opinion one way or the other," said the New York Republican, who also is a member of the Senate Finance Committee.
"At this point ... it's not a high priority issue" for the Senate, said D'Amato, in a breakfast address at a Government Finance Officers Association conference here.
"We have lots of things to do," D'Amato said. But "we'll look at it. We'll discuss it. We are going to listen to all the facts."
D'Amato was referring to a bill to curb stadium financing reoffered this month by Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, D-New York.

In other comments, D'Amato said he would back any upcoming efforts on Capitol Hill to relax caps on tax-exempt spending by state and local governments, but warned municipalities not to count on a cooperative Congress.

"I would support efforts to broaden them and give greater discretion to states to fund these projects and use tax exempt financing and tax credits,". There should be an adjustment," D'Amato said, concerning current Internal Revenue Service spending caps on tax-exempt bond financing by municipalities.
"Do I believe it will pass? Probably not," he said. Some members of Congress are not "very sympathetic to states and local governments," said D'Amato, a long-time backer of tax-exempt finance.
"Some of the spending caps that have been put on the use of tax-exempt financing are arbitrary and unnecessarily restrictive and hurt economic development," D'Amato said.
D'Amato also said state and local governments should be prepared for a fight on Capitol Hill over their ability to continue to issue tax-exempt bonds.
"Will the battle be on? Of course," D'Amato said.

"Obviously, in any plan that calls for a fairer, flatter tax, they are going to have to raise revenue," D'Amato said. "And you will obviously be down here again lobbying frenetically to save your tax-exempt status as it relates to muni bonds."
